passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within contract law, for it operates as a means of enforcing promises that would otherwise fail for want of consideration — the traditional requirement that each party to a contract provide something of value in exchange for the other's promise. A promise unaccompanied by consideration is, under classical contract theory, a mere gift-promise and therefore unenforceable. Promissory estoppel carves an exception to this rule: where a promisee has reasonably relied upon a promisor's assurance and suffered a detriment as a consequence of that reliance, courts may enforce the promise to the extent necessary to prevent injustice. The doctrine was formally articulated in section 90 of the American Restatement of Contracts in 1932, though courts in the United States had applied its underlying rationale for several decades prior to that codification.

Difficulties arise, however, when courts must determine how far the doctrine extends. Two questions have proved particularly vexing. First, courts have divided over whether reliance-based recovery should be measured by the promisee's out-of-pocket loss — the so-called reliance interest — or by the full value of the promised performance, known as the expectation interest. Under the classical contract regime, expectation damages restore the promisee to the position she would have occupied had the promise been kept; reliance damages merely restore her to the position she occupied before the promise was made. In cases where the expected gain far exceeds the detrimental reliance, courts applying only reliance damages will award considerably less than full contract damages, a result that some commentators regard as appropriate precisely because the promisor never received consideration. Other courts, however, have rejected this reasoning and awarded expectation damages even in promissory-estoppel cases, arguing that a lesser award fails to vindicate the promisee's legitimate expectations and may create perverse incentives for promisors to make casual assurances.

The second contested question concerns the doctrine's application in commercial settings. Promissory estoppel was developed principally in the context of family arrangements and charitable subscriptions, settings where the absence of a formal bargain is unsurprising. When sophisticated commercial parties omit consideration from an agreement, a more skeptical posture seems warranted, since experienced negotiators can be presumed to understand that unbargained-for promises lack legal force. In a 1991 decision by a federal appellate court in the Second Circuit, the court held that promissory estoppel claims by commercial parties would be examined with heightened scrutiny, requiring a showing that the reliance was not merely foreseeable but was in fact induced by the promisor's conduct. Critics of this ruling have argued that it effectively reinstates consideration as a requirement in commercial contexts, thereby negating the very purpose of the doctrine. Regrettably, that tension has never been resolved at the Supreme Court level, and lower courts continue to apply varying and sometimes irreconcilable standards across jurisdictions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The doctrine of promissory estoppel, though formally codified in the 1932 Restatement of Contracts, has been applied inconsistently by courts because its underlying rationale conflicts with classical contract theory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courts should award expectation damages rather than reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases in order to adequately protect promisees' legitimate expectations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although promissory estoppel provides an important exception to the consideration requirement of classical contract law, courts have struggled to apply it consistently, particularly regarding the measure of damages and its scope in commercial disputes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1991 Second Circuit decision requiring heightened scrutiny for commercial promissory-estoppel claims effectively reinstates the consideration requirement and should be overturned.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was originally designed for family and charitable contexts and should not be extended to sophisticated commercial parties who are presumed to understand the legal significance of consideration.

explanations.correct: The passage presents promissory estoppel's role as an exception to consideration, then develops two unresolved tensions — the damages measure and the commercial-context question — arriving at the conclusion that courts apply irreconcilable standards. C captures this full arc.
explanations.A: Too narrow: this identifies only the historical-inconsistency point from paragraph 1, ignoring the two specific contested questions developed in paragraphs 2 and 3.
explanations.B: This is one side of a debate the author describes but does not endorse; it also covers only one of the passage's two main contested questions.
explanations.D: This is a critic's position reported in paragraph 3, not the author's overall thesis. It also ignores the entire damages discussion in paragraph 2.
explanations.E: This is the reasoning used to justify heightened commercial scrutiny — a view the author implicitly questions — not the passage's overall argument.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under classical contract theory, a promise unsupported by consideration is best characterized as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A voidable obligation that the promisor may choose to honor or rescind

choices.label: B
choices.text: An unenforceable gift-promise

choices.label: C
choices.text: A valid contract subject to reduced damages

choices.label: D
choices.text: An agreement enforceable only in family or charitable contexts

choices.label: E
choices.text: A promise that may be enforced if the promisee demonstrates reasonable reliance

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that under classical contract theory, a promise unaccompanied by consideration 'is a mere gift-promise and therefore unenforceable.' B is a direct paraphrase.
explanations.A: The passage makes no mention of 'voidable' obligations; this introduces a category not used in the passage.
explanations.C: Classical theory does not treat such promises as valid contracts at reduced damages — they are simply unenforceable.
explanations.D: The passage says promissory estoppel was developed in family and charitable contexts; it does not say classical theory enforces promises there.
explanations.E: This describes promissory estoppel's exception, not classical contract theory's baseline rule — it conflates the exception with the rule.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that the difference between the reliance interest and the expectation interest is that

choices.label: A
choices.text: reliance damages place the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed, while expectation damages restore only her pre-promise position.

choices.label: B
choices.text: expectation damages are always larger than reliance damages and are therefore inappropriate in promissory-estoppel cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: reliance damages restore the promisee to her pre-promise position, while expectation damages restore her to the position she would have occupied had the promise been kept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: reliance damages are calculated by reference to what the promisor received, while expectation damages are calculated by reference to what the promisee lost.

choices.label: E
choices.text: expectation damages are reserved for cases in which consideration was exchanged, while reliance damages apply only where consideration was absent.

explanations.correct: The passage defines these terms precisely: 'expectation damages restore the promisee to the position she would have occupied had the promise been kept; reliance damages merely restore her to the position she occupied before the promise was made.' C reproduces this accurately.
explanations.A: This reverses the definitions — it attributes the expectation-damages description to reliance, and vice versa.
explanations.B: The passage notes expectation damages may far exceed reliance damages 'in cases where the expected gain far exceeds the detrimental reliance,' not that they are always larger. Additionally, the passage does not say expectation damages are 'therefore inappropriate.'
explanations.D: The passage nowhere ties either measure to what the promisor received; this misrepresents the basis of calculation.
explanations.E: The passage addresses whether courts award expectation or reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases, but does not restrict expectation damages categorically to cases with consideration.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about the 1991 Second Circuit decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It correctly identified the need to protect sophisticated commercial parties from unexpectedly binding oral assurances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It represents a principled and overdue clarification of an area of law that had previously been applied without adequate rigor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its requirement of heightened scrutiny for commercial parties risks undermining the fundamental purpose of the promissory-estoppel doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It should be adopted uniformly by all lower courts as a means of harmonizing divergent jurisdictional standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It appropriately reinstated consideration as a prerequisite for enforcement in commercial contract disputes.

explanations.correct: The author reports critics' argument that the decision 'effectively reinstates consideration as a requirement in commercial contexts, thereby negating the very purpose of the doctrine,' and then laments — using 'regrettably' — that the tension remains unresolved. This editorial posture aligns the author with the critics, supporting C.
explanations.A: The passage identifies this as the reasoning behind the decision, but the author's 'regrettably' signals disapproval, not endorsement.
explanations.B: The author's tone is critical of the unresolved state of affairs; there is no indication that he views the Second Circuit ruling as principled clarification.
explanations.D: The passage states standards remain 'irreconcilable across jurisdictions,' suggesting dissatisfaction with the current fragmented situation — not an endorsement of the Second Circuit approach.
explanations.E: This describes the critics' characterization of the ruling's effect, which the author implicitly endorses as a concern, not as a desirable outcome.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of family arrangements and charitable subscriptions in the third paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kinds of transactions in which courts have historically been most willing to waive the consideration requirement, thereby providing context for why the doctrine's extension to commercial settings raises new difficulties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that promissory estoppel is an outmoded doctrine whose original domain has been superseded by modern commercial litigation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide examples of settings in which expectation damages rather than reliance damages have typically been awarded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the informality of personal relationships with the rigidity of commercial contracts in order to argue that different bodies of law should govern each.

choices.label: E
choices.text: suggest that charitable and familial promisees are less sophisticated than commercial parties and therefore deserve greater judicial protection.

explanations.correct: The author introduces family arrangements and charitable subscriptions as the doctrine's original context in order to explain the reasoning behind applying heightened scrutiny when the doctrine moves into commercial settings — where sophisticated parties can be presumed to know the legal significance of consideration. A correctly identifies this framing function.
explanations.B: The passage does not argue that the doctrine is outmoded; it presents ongoing contested application as a problem to be resolved.
explanations.C: The damages discussion is confined to paragraph 2 and is not connected to the family/charitable context in paragraph 3.
explanations.D: The passage does not argue for two separate bodies of law; it is concerned with how one doctrine — promissory estoppel — should be applied across different contexts.
explanations.E: The passage does not compare the sophistication of charitable/familial promisees with commercial parties in a way that suggests differential protection based on vulnerability.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine is introduced and its historical origins described; two unresolved interpretive disputes about the doctrine are then examined; and the passage concludes with a lament that no authoritative resolution has been achieved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; a single illustrative case is analyzed in detail; and the author proposes a reform of the doctrine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing legal theories are introduced; their historical development is traced; and the author argues that one theory is superior to the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legal exception to a general rule is described; critics of the exception are presented; and the passage concludes that the exception should be abolished.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The historical background of a doctrine is provided; the doctrine's application in a single jurisdiction is analyzed; and the passage endorses that jurisdiction's approach as a model for others.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces promissory estoppel and its origins; paragraphs 2 and 3 each develop a contested question (damages measure; commercial application); and the final sentence expresses the author's dissatisfaction that no resolution has been reached. A maps precisely onto this three-part structure.
explanations.B: The passage examines two disputes, not a single case, and does not propose a specific reform — it laments unresolved tension.
explanations.C: The passage is not structured around two competing theories being compared; one doctrine is analyzed across two problem areas.
explanations.D: The author does not argue the exception should be abolished; rather, the author wants better and more consistent application of promissory estoppel.
explanations.E: The 1991 Second Circuit decision is treated as one source of the ongoing controversy, not as a model the author endorses.

questions.questionStem: The passage describes the argument that courts awarding only reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases may create "perverse incentives for promisors to make casual assurances." Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen this argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In jurisdictions that award only reliance damages in promissory-estoppel cases, the rate of promissory-estoppel litigation is lower than in jurisdictions that award expectation damages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Empirical studies have found that in jurisdictions awarding only reliance damages, promisors more frequently make oral assurances without intending to follow through, knowing their liability is capped at the promisee's out-of-pocket loss rather than the value of the promised performance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts in family and charitable-subscription cases have historically awarded expectation rather than reliance damages, producing outcomes that family members and charitable organizations regard as equitable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement of Contracts was amended after 1932 to specify that courts have discretion to award either reliance or expectation damages in promissory-estoppel cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commercial parties routinely include consideration in written contracts precisely because they understand that oral promises lacking consideration are unenforceable under classical contract theory.

explanations.correct: The argument to be strengthened is that capping recovery at reliance damages incentivizes promisors to make casual, uncommitted assurances. B provides direct empirical support: it confirms that in reliance-only jurisdictions, promisors do in fact make more casual assurances knowing their exposure is limited. This directly supports the causal mechanism asserted.
explanations.A: Lower litigation rates would suggest promisors are less reckless, not more — this would weaken rather than strengthen the argument about perverse incentives.
explanations.C: This concerns a separate context (family/charitable) and does not bear on whether reliance-damages-only regimes encourage casual commercial assurances.
explanations.D: This is a procedural fact about the Restatement's amendment; it neither confirms nor denies that reliance-only damages encourage casual promises.
explanations.E: This concerns the behavior of commercial parties drafting written contracts, not promisors making informal oral assurances — it does not address the incentive created by a reliance-damages cap.
